title: Multicritical dissipative phase transitions manipulated by dipole--dipole interactions
authors: Jia-Xin Wang, Qian Bin, Jing-Jing Cao, Xin-You Lü
abstract: Precise control of criticality in superradiant phase transitions is essential for quantum state engineering and the simulation of nonequilibrium phase transitions. Here, we investigate theoretically multicritical phenomena in a dissipative two-Rydberg-atom cavity--QED system. The intrinisic dipole--dipole interaction between the two Rydberg atoms restructures the energy-level landscape of the atomic subsystem, thereby significantly modifying the boundary of the continuous second-order superradiant phase transition, and shifting both the phase boundary and the multicritical point toward weaker atom--cavity strengths. For sufficiently strong dipole--dipole interactions, the continuous second-order phase transition and the multicritical point both disappear, leaving only a discontinuous first--order phase transition that enables the emergence of a superradiant phase even at arbitrarily weak atom--cavity coupling. This work is of fundamental interest for studying dissipative quantum phase transitions, with potential implications for quantum precision measurement and quantum sensing.
summary: The paper theoretically examines superradiant phase transitions in a two-Rydberg-atom cavity QED system, focusing on the role of dipole-dipole interactions. It demonstrates that these interactions can restructure the energy landscape, causing continuous second-order transitions to vanish entirely. This mechanism allows for robust superradiance even when atom-cavity coupling is extremely weak.
main_problem: The study investigates how intrinsic dipole-dipole interactions modify multicritical dissipative phase transitions occurring during superradiant phase transitions.
main_result: Strong dipole-dipole interactions can eliminate the continuous second-order transition and its associated critical point, leaving only a first-order transition that sustains superradiance even with weak atom-cavity coupling.
method: The analysis employs the Heisenberg–Langevin formalism combined with mean-field approximations and subsequent quantum fluctuation analysis to determine steady states and stability boundaries.
model_or_system: The system is a cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) setup involving two interacting Rydberg atoms coupled to a single cavity mode. The dynamics are governed by an effective Hamiltonian incorporating dipole-dipole interactions ($V \propto 1/R^3$).
key_observables: Cavity field amplitude ($\alpha$), phase boundaries (first-order and second-order), and the Wigner function distribution.
important_parameters: Dipole–dipole interaction strength ($V$), atom-cavity coupling strengths ($\lambda_{x,j}, \lambda_{y,j}$), and cavity decay rate ($\kappa$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the mean-field approximation supplemented by quantum fluctuation analysis, using the Heisenberg–Langevin formalism for dynamics.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the model; panels (b) and (c) illustrate how varying $V/\omega$ shifts and alters the boundaries between first-order and second-order phase transitions in terms of the real part of the cavity field amplitude ($\alpha_{Re}$).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework using the Hamiltonian, derives mean-field equations via Langevin formalism, performs stability analysis on fluctuations to map out phase boundaries, and concludes by discussing the physical implications for quantum control.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium quantum dynamics in cavity QED systems, showing how controllable interactions can fundamentally alter critical points, which is highly relevant for designing quantum sensors and simulators.
